items.item: A barrier riding the same channels as ordinary records, rather than a separate control plane, is what lets Flink take a globally consistent snapshot without ever pausing the dataflow to do it — the exact property Chandy and Lamport's original algorithm was designed to generalize beyond request-response systems.

at.step: Reveal: a barrier rides the stream like Chandy and Lamport's snapshot

items.item: Aligned checkpointing's stall under backpressure isn't an implementation gap to fix later — it follows directly from the correctness requirement (every input must have passed the same logical point) the mechanism exists to satisfy in the first place.

at.step: Reveal: aligned checkpoints wait for every input

items.item: Unaligned checkpointing doesn't eliminate the cost of a backed-up channel, it relocates it — from stalled wall-clock time to a larger recorded snapshot — which is why it's a trade-off a job opts into deliberately, not a strictly better default.

at.step: Reveal: unaligned checkpoints snapshot on first sight

items.item: Bounding checkpoint cost by the delta rather than the accumulated total is the same idea this chapter's compacted-topic and retention discussions apply to storage, now applied to the cost of fault tolerance itself.

at.step: Reveal: incremental checkpoints are bounded by the delta

items.item: Stating exactly-once as the default, with at-least-once as a narrow, named exception for genuinely latency-sensitive jobs, matters because the cheaper mode's risk (occasional double-processing on recovery) is silent until a recovery actually happens.

at.step: Reveal: exactly-once is the default; at-least-once is the rare exception

items.item: The checkpoint/savepoint distinction being about ownership and intent, not just mechanism, is what lets a job survive a deliberate version or parallelism change that an ordinary checkpoint was never designed to carry across.

at.step: Reveal: a checkpoint is automatic; a savepoint is deliberate
